scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a qualified position granting that beginners bring fresh ideas while arguing that experts make most contributions; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Fresh eyes can sometimes notice what trained experts overlook.
Some people argue that in any field the beginner is more likely than the expert to make important contributions.
I agree that beginners occasionally bring valuable new ideas, but I disagree that they are generally more likely than experts to advance a field.
First, beginners do enjoy one real advantage, which is freedom from fixed assumptions.
Because they have not yet learned what is considered impossible, they are sometimes willing to ask bold questions.
For example, young scientists in their twenties have occasionally proposed ideas that older specialists had dismissed as unrealistic.
This shows that a fresh perspective can break through habits of thought that hold a field back.
Newcomers are also less afraid of failure, since they have no reputation to protect.
A willingness to take risks can lead to surprising and original work.
In this limited sense, beginners can indeed make important contributions.
Second, however, the great majority of important contributions still come from experts.
Deep knowledge is usually what allows a person to see exactly where a field is stuck and how to move it forward.
Consider the years of study a doctor needs before she can safely test a new treatment or interpret a confusing result.
Such expertise is what turns a vague idea into a discovery that others can trust and build upon.
Most beginners, by contrast, simply lack the background to know which questions are worth asking.
Their fresh ideas, however appealing, often repeat mistakes that specialists settled long ago.
On balance, then, sustained knowledge contributes far more than inexperience does.
In conclusion, beginners can offer fresh perspectives that experts sometimes miss.
But important contributions usually depend on the deep understanding that only experience can provide.
The most progress is likely to come not from beginners alone, but from experts who manage to keep a beginner's open mind.
